argument:
The bear correctly requires the dividend deduction and gross-credit deterioration to remain visible. However, disclosed CET1 of 15.657% and total capital of 19.413% establish a substantial measured starting cushion; the analysis need not rely on an unverified capital assumption. Net impairment moved from 0.79% to 0.80%, while cost restraint kept H1 profit almost stable despite weaker income.

At 11.51x trailing earnings and a vendor-reported 6.2% yield, ownership offers an observed income proposition rather than requiring rapid growth or multiple expansion. That yield is not guaranteed total return, and post-dividend capital should be checked. The positive case is resilient distributable earnings within disclosed capital capacity; continued impairment or revenue erosion would weaken it. Negative momentum supports patient entry without erasing the income economics.
key_points: Capital is quantified, with proposed dividend deduction still relevant.
Limited net-impairment movement and cost restraint support earnings resilience.
Yield offers conditional income compensation rather than a recovery guarantee.
rebuttal_to_previous: Rising gross impairment is adverse, but the 0.80% net-impaired ratio and disclosed capital provide a measured cushion. I retain the dividend-deduction qualification rather than claiming risk-free payout; the 6.2% reported yield supplies a concrete income case despite weak growth.
